10094-a-soldier-of-virginia-a-tale-of-co:
Burton Egbert Stevenson's 1901 novel, dedicated to the gallant men who fell with the dust of failure bitter on their lips, tells of Colonel Washington and Braddock's defeat. It opens with Lieutenant Allen growing insulting, the story of Fontenoy, and a narrator introducing himself.

The ending of a honeymoon, the secret of a heart, and a decision to be a soldier follow. Then come a ride to Williamsburg, a first taste of warfare, the French scoring first, and Dorothy making her choice. Stevenson writes colonial adventure with care. Readers get the French and Indian War through young Virginian eyes.
12460-pomona-s-travels-a-series-of-lette:
Frank R. Stockton's 1894 letters follow Pomona, former handmaiden to the mistress of Rudder Grange, on travels in England. Illustrated by A. B. Frost, the letters run from Wanted, a Vicarage and On the Four-in-hand to a cottage at Chedcombe, a lodger, Americanisms expounded, a hayfield and a runaway tricycle.

Pomona writes home in a lively, practical voice, with Jone beside her, teaching young ladies to rake, sliding backward down the slope of centuries and stag-hunting on a tricycle. Stockton's humour lies in an American servant's eye on English custom. The book is a light, affectionate sequel, best enjoyed as a string of comic travel letters.
19807-sketch-of-grammar-of-the-chippeway:
Chippeway is an older name for the Ojibwe language. A Sketch of Grammar of the Chippeway Languages sets out its rules for English readers. It adds a vocabulary to the grammar. Sample lines give the Lord's Prayer in Chippeway spelling. Phrases like Ish-pe-ming a-yah-yun render 'who art in heaven.' The orthography follows missionary practice of its day.

Grammar sketches like this were tools for missionaries and traders. They froze a spoken language into print rules. Modern linguists mine them for older forms and sounds. The spellings look rough beside today's Ojibwe orthographies. Still, they preserve words as elders spoke them then. Such books are primary sources for language revival work.
22291-odd:
Amy Le Feuvre called this children's story simply Odd. Its heroine Betty earns the name by her ways. One adventure goes wrong in a familiar Le Feuvre scene: Betty's head goes out through a gap easily enough, but will not come back in. Nurse comes to the rescue with an angry hand, and the poor little head is bruised in the pulling.

Her reward is an aching head and dry bread for tea. Around such scrapes Le Feuvre builds her lessons of patience, truth, and trust in God. She wrote for children who liked a heroine with spirit and faults. Odd is a small, characteristic piece of her large and once-beloved output.
22681-the-life-and-public-service-of-gen:
Abraham Lincoln delivered this address on the life and public service of General Zachary Taylor, the president who died in office in 1850. The catalog record gives no year. A citizens' committee in Lincoln's city chose him to speak at City Hall on the late president, and the pamphlet prints the invitation along with the speech.

The letter in the text asks the chosen speaker to address fellow citizens on the life of Z. Taylor, late President of the United States. Lincoln, then a former congressman in private practice, answered with a measured eulogy of the old soldier-president. The piece is minor beside his later speeches, yet it shows his care with public mourning and with the character of a Whig hero. Collectors of Lincoln's writings prize such early, occasional pieces.
23866-the-house-that-jack-built-a-game-o:
E. Marshall of Fleet Street, London, published The House That Jack Built as a game of forfeits, priced at one shilling and embellished with engravings. Its cumulative rhyme builds verse by verse, each picture adding a link to the chain.

This is the house that Jack built, then the malt that lay in the house, the rat that ate the malt, and the cat that killed the rat. A dog, a cow with a crumpled horn, a maiden all forlorn, and a man all tattered and torn follow in turn. To the rhyme Marshall adds the entertaining fable of The Magpie. It is a nursery classic in chapbook form, made to be chanted and played.
32505-the-systematics-of-the-frogs-of-th:
Juan R. León's study revises the frogs of the Hyla rubra group in Middle America. It was published by the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History in volume eighteen, number six, pages 505 to 545, on December 2, 1969. With seven figures and four plates, it gives keys to species, subspecies, and known tadpoles, followed by full accounts of each form. Species treated include Hyla boulengeri, Hyla foliamorta, Hyla rubra, Hyla elaeochroa, and Hyla staufferi with its subspecies.

León examined 1,383 preserved specimens, fifty skeletons, and nine lots of tadpoles, using twelve measurements and six proportions from current anuran systematics. A closing section traces evolutionary history, with literature cited. The paper suits herpetologists and students who need a careful, specimen-based revision of a Middle American frog group.
34270-barbara-ladd:
Charles Roberts, who wrote The Kindred of the Wild, stands behind this tale of a bold young girl. Page printed Barbara Ladd in October 1902, with plates by Frank Verbeck. Eight printings by 1908 prove the book's hold on readers.

The front plate shows Barbara leaning from a porch to drop a bundle into a bed of marigolds. She opens the tale at her window at night, wide-eyed and still. Fear of the dark is the one thing that can daunt her wild, daring spirit, the tale says. Other plates show Doctor John vowing that Barbara has led Mehitable astray, and a man sinking back into Barbara's arms. Mischief and heart fill this Canadian tale.
45185-burritt-college-centennial-celebra:
Burritt College Centennial Celebration preserves the centennial address of Charles Lee Lewis, of the class of 1903, delivered on August 14, 1948. The gathering marked one hundred years since the college's founding. Lewis opens with Daniel Webster's saying on Dartmouth College: it is a little college, but there are those who love it.

Turning back the clock to 1848, Lewis sketches a rough and isolated country. Van Buren County was only about eight years old, and Spencer was a small village. Roads were so poor that trips to Sparta or McMinnville took hours. The railway was still under construction, and no Vanderbilt, Sewanee, or Peabody College yet existed. Tennessee had been a state only fifty-two years, and the Nashville capitol was unfinished.
53518-right-tackle-todd:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Right Tackle Todd, a school football novel published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1924. Leslie Crump drew the pictures. The book belongs to a series of eleven football novels, one for each position on the team. Its hero is Jim Todd, who plays right tackle for Alton school.

The chapter list promises a full school year of sport and trouble. Jim quits, buys a football, and asks a loan. He studies the art of line playing and visits a police station and a judge's chamber. A thief in the dormitory troubles the boys. The front picture shows Jim tired, happy, and feeling foolish. The season builds toward the match with Kenly Hall and a bandaged hand.
56056-the-young-circus-rider-or-the-myst: Horatio Alger wrote this boys tale in his Atlantic series of books. Coates printed the Alger books in Philadelphia in cloth sets. The tale joins Do and Dare and Hector Inheritance in that set. Front lists span Ragged Dick, Tattered Tom, and Luck and Pluck sets, all famed boys books of their day.
64851-decidedly-odd:
Edwin Balmer and William MacHarg wrote Decidedly Odd, a Luther Trant mystery tale for magazine readers. Trant, a psychologist, sits in his office on a rainy April morning reading fiction with a pulse machine strapped to his wrist. The device traces his blood wave on smoked paper as he reads each page with close care.

Trant notes how the line flattens when interest grips him and swells at a sharp incident. A phone call from Cuthbert Edwards breaks in with alarm about a cipher notice and a missing son. Mind reading by machine meets detective work as the plot unfolds from that urgent call for help. Readers get an early mix of science, psychology, and crime in the Trant series, both odd and clever.
72058-amos-judd:
Mitchell tells a quiet tale in Amos Judd, printed in New York in 1901 with drawings in color by Keller. The book bears copyright dates of 1895 and 1901 from Scribner. Plates show talks of wealth, a startled apology, and a man who thanks Bull for a chase.

The tale opens at Bingham Cross Roads station in hot September sun. Four folk leave the train. A woman with bundles walks fast for the village, sure of her way. The rest are three strangers: two men and a small boy. Their dark skin and strange air draw stares from the car. Folk watch them with doubt as they take their bearings on the platform.
a-soldier-of-virginia-a-tale-of-colonel-: Burton Egbert Stevenson tells a tale of Colonel Washington at Braddock's defeat in this 1901 novel. It is dedicated to the gallant men who fell with the dust of failure bitter on their lips. The narrator introduces himself, decides to be a soldier, rides to Williamsburg, and tastes warfare as the French score first. Through Riverview, Dorothy's choice, a weary journey, and the lesson of the wilderness, defeat becomes dishonour and Braddock pays the price.
britannica-1911-lydd:
Lydd, a market town in Kent, England, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies in the open lowland of Romney Marsh, near the shingle point of Dungeness. Its count in 1901 was 2,675 people. Its church of All Saints has a fine late Gothic tower with rich vault work inside.

The land round Lydd feeds large flocks of sheep. A camp with gun and rifle ranges stands on the Rypes near by. That camp gave its name to the blast powder called lyddite. The first town grew at a fishing post, then became a port of some note. Shore shifts have left it near three miles inland. In 1290 it gained the rights of the Cinque Ports.
britannica-1911-rudd:
Rudd, or red eye, is a fish of the carp family, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short nature entry. It is spread over Europe, north and south of the Alps, and is found in Asia Minor as well. It is common where there are still waters with muddy bottoms. 

The rudd and the roach are very alike, and anglers often confuse them. The rudd is told apart chiefly by its dorsal fin, which sits farther back on the body. It is a fine fish but little esteemed for food, and it rarely passes a foot in length. It feeds on small freshwater animals and soft plant matter, and it spawns in April or May.
britannica-1911-sudd:
Sudd, or Sadd, an Arabic word meaning to dam, names the plant barrier that has at times closed the Upper Nile to boats, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article describes it. The barrier is made of masses of papyrus and a reed called um suf. Earth clings to the roots of those reeds. Small swimming plants and the light, brittle ambach are mixed in as well.

The reeds grow thickly along the Nile banks and lagoons. Storms loosen them, and they drift until they lodge and form a dam across the channel. Fresh arrivals build the blocks out, sometimes for miles. The packed mass, like peat, is so firm that men can walk over it, and in places even elephants could cross. At length the water pressure opens a side channel or bursts the sudd.
pomona-s-travels-a-series-of-letters-to-:
Frank R. Stockton published Pomona's Travels in 1894, illustrated by A. B. Frost, as a sequel in spirit to his beloved Rudder Grange. The form is letters: Pomona, once the handmaiden of Rudder Grange, writes home to her former mistress from a tour of England with her husband Jone. Her first letter announces the errand with perfect Pomona logic: she wants a vicarage, and has come to England to look at how the English manage such things.

Letters follow on the four-in-hand coach, a cottage at Chedcombe, a lodger taken in, and Jone overshadowing a waiter, each episode filtered through Pomona's shrewd, funny, semi-lettered voice. Stockton's humor depends on her dignity: a servant girl touring the mother country as a lady of leisure, reporting its wonders deadpan. Frost's drawings complete the portrait of one of American humor's most original narrators.
